title: Part 2, Chapter 70
paragraphs: Which follows sixty-nine and deals with matters essential to a clear understanding of this history

Sancho slept that night on a cot in the same room as Don Quixote — an arrangement he would gladly have avoided if he could, since he knew perfectly well that his master would keep him awake with questions and answers, and he was in no mood for conversation; the pain of his recent martyrdom was still with him and put a damper on his free use of his tongue. He would rather have slept alone in a hovel than in that splendid room with company. His fear proved well founded and his prediction exactly right, for his master had barely gotten into bed before he said, “What do you make of tonight’s adventure, Sancho? Great and mighty is the power of cold-hearted disdain, for you have seen with your own eyes Altisidora struck dead — not by arrows, not by the sword or any weapon of war, not by deadly poison, but purely by the thought of the severity and scorn with which I have always treated her.”

“She was welcome to die,” said Sancho, “whenever she liked and however she liked — and she could have left me out of it, because I never made her fall in love and I never scorned her. I don’t know, and I can’t begin to imagine, how the recovery of Altisidora, a girl with more fancies than sense, can have anything to do — as I’ve said before — with the sufferings of Sancho Panza. Now I’m starting to see plainly and clearly that there really are enchanters and enchanted people in this world; and may God deliver me from them, since I can’t deliver myself. So I beg your worship to let me sleep and not ask me any more questions, unless you want me to throw myself out the window.”
“Sleep, Sancho my friend,” said Don Quixote, “if the pinpricks and pinches you have received, and the smacks dealt out to you, will allow it.”

“No pain could match the insult of those smacks,” said Sancho, “for the simple reason that it was duennas — curse them — who gave them to me. But once again I beg your worship to let me sleep, because sleep is relief from misery for those who are miserable while awake.”
“So be it, and God be with you,” said Don Quixote.

They both fell asleep, and Cide Hamete, the author of this great history, took the opportunity to set down and explain what had moved the duke and duchess to mount the elaborate scheme just described. The bachelor Samson Carrasco, he says, had not forgotten how, as the Knight of the Mirrors, he had been beaten and brought down by Don Quixote — a defeat and overthrow that wrecked all his plans — and he resolved to try again, hoping for better luck this time. So, having learned where Don Quixote was from the page who carried the letter and the present to Sancho’s wife, Teresa Panza, he equipped himself with new armor and another horse, put a white moon on his shield, and had his arms carried on a mule led by a peasant — not by Tom Cecial, his former squire, for fear Sancho or Don Quixote might recognize him. He arrived at the duke’s castle, and the duke told him the road and route Don Quixote had taken, intending to attend the jousts at Saragossa. He also told him about the practical jokes he had played on him, including the scheme for disenchanting Dulcinea at the expense of Sancho’s backside; and finally he recounted the trick Sancho had played on his master, convincing him that Dulcinea was enchanted and transformed into a peasant girl, and how the duchess, his wife, had persuaded Sancho that he was the one deceived, since Dulcinea really was enchanted. At all this the bachelor laughed heartily, marveling equally at Sancho’s mixture of cunning and simplicity and at the extremes Don Quixote’s madness could reach. The duke asked him, if he found Don Quixote — whether he defeated him or not — to come back that way and report the outcome. The bachelor did so. He set out in search of Don Quixote, and not finding him at Saragossa he pressed on, and what happened to him then has already been told. He returned to the duke’s castle and gave him the whole story — the terms of the combat, and how Don Quixote, like a loyal knight-errant, was now on his way home to keep his promise of withdrawing to his village for a year, by the end of which, the bachelor said, he might perhaps be cured of his madness; for that was the purpose behind all these disguises, since it was a pitiable thing that a gentleman of such fine qualities as Don Quixote should be a madman. With that he took his leave of the duke and went home to his village to wait for Don Quixote, who was following behind him. This gave the duke his opening for the present hoax — so much did he relish everything to do with Sancho and Don Quixote. He posted large numbers of his servants, on foot and on horseback, along all the roads near and far around the castle, wherever he thought Don Quixote might pass on his way home, with orders to bring him to the castle by fair means or foul if they found him. They did find him, and sent word to the duke, who had already decided what was to be done; the moment he heard of his arrival he ordered the torches and lamps in the courtyard lit and Altisidora laid on the catafalque with all the pomp and ceremony already described — the whole production so well staged and acted that it was barely distinguishable from the real thing. And Cide Hamete adds that, for his part, he considers the perpetrators of the joke as crazy as its victims, and that the duke and duchess came within two fingers’ breadth of looking like fools themselves, taking such pains to make fools of a pair of fools.

As for that pair, one was sleeping soundly and the other lying awake with his rambling thoughts when daylight reached them, and with it the urge to get up; for lounging in soft bedding never appealed to Don Quixote, victorious or vanquished. Altisidora — back from death to life, as Don Quixote imagined — keeping up her lord and lady’s whim, came into the room crowned with the same garland she had worn on the catafalque, dressed in a robe of white taffeta embroidered with golden flowers, her hair loose over her shoulders, leaning on a staff of fine black ebony. Don Quixote, flustered and embarrassed by her appearance, shrank down and all but buried himself under the sheets and bedspread, his tongue tied, unable to offer her so much as a courtesy. Altisidora sat down on a chair at the head of the bed and, after a deep sigh, said to him in a faint, gentle voice, “When women of rank and modest maidens trample their honor underfoot and give free rein to the tongue that breaks through every restraint, broadcasting the innermost secrets of their hearts, they are driven to desperate straits. I am such a one, Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha — crushed, conquered, lovestruck, yet for all that patient in suffering and virtuous, so much so that my heart broke under my grief and I lost my life. For the past two days I have been dead, slain by the thought of the cruelty with which you have treated me, you unbending knight,
O you, harder than marble to my cry;

or at least everyone who saw me believed I was dead; and if Love had not taken pity on me and staked my recovery on the sufferings of this good squire, I would have stayed in the other world for good.”

“Love could just as easily have staked it on the sufferings of my donkey, and I’d have thanked him for it,” said Sancho. “But tell me, señora — and may heaven send you a more tender-hearted lover than my master — what did you see in the other world? What goes on in hell? Because that’s where anyone who dies in despair is bound to end up.”

“To tell you the truth,” said Altisidora, “I can’t have died completely, because I never went inside hell — if I had gone in, it’s quite certain I could never have gotten out again, no matter what I did. The truth is, I came as far as the gate, where a dozen or so devils were playing tennis, all in breeches and doublets, with falling collars trimmed with Flemish lace and matching ruffles serving as wristbands, leaving four fingers’ width of arm bare to make their hands look longer. They held rackets of fire in their hands; but what amazed me more was that instead of tennis balls they used books, apparently stuffed with wind and rubbish — a strange and marvelous thing. Yet even that did not astonish me as much as noticing that, although it is normal among players for the winners to be happy and the losers annoyed, in that game everyone was growling, everyone was snarling, and everyone was cursing everyone else.” “That’s no surprise,” said Sancho, “because devils, playing or not, can never be content, win or lose.”

“Very likely,” said Altisidora; “but there is something else that surprises me too — I mean it surprised me at the time — which is that no ball survived its first stroke or could be used a second time; and it was remarkable how the books kept coming, new ones and old ones, in constant supply. To one of them, a brand-new, handsomely bound volume, they gave such a whack that they knocked its insides out and scattered its pages everywhere. ‘See what book that is,’ one devil said to another, and the other answered, ‘It is the “Second Part of the History of Don Quixote of La Mancha” — not the one by Cide Hamete, the original author, but by an Aragonese who claims to be from Tordesillas.’ ‘Get it out of here,’ said the first, ‘and into the depths of hell with it, out of my sight.’ ‘Is it that bad?’ said the other. ‘So bad,’ said the first, ‘that if I had deliberately set out to write a worse one, I couldn’t have managed it.’ They went on with their game, batting other books around; and I, having heard them speak the name of Don Quixote, whom I love and adore so much, took care to fix this vision in my memory.”

“A vision is surely what it was,” said Don Quixote, “for there is no other I in the world. That history has been passing from hand to hand around here for some time, though it never stays long in any, because everyone gives it a kick on its way. It does not trouble me to hear that I am drifting about as a phantom shape in the darkness of the pit or in the daylight above, because I am not the man that history is about. If it is good, faithful, and true, it will live for ages; but if it is bad, the road from its birth to its burial will not be a long one.”

Altisidora was about to continue her complaint against Don Quixote when he said to her, “I have told you many times, señora, how it grieves me that you have set your affections on me, since from mine they can receive only gratitude, never a return. I was born to belong to Dulcinea del Toboso, and the fates — if fates there are — dedicated me to her; to suppose that any other beauty could take the place she holds in my heart is to suppose an impossibility. This plain declaration should be enough to make you retreat within the bounds of your modesty, for no one can be bound to do the impossible.”

At this, Altisidora, with a show of anger and agitation, burst out, “By God’s life, Don Codfish, soul of a mortar, stone of a date, more stubborn and unyielding than a peasant asked a favor when his mind is already made up — if I get my hands on you I’ll scratch your eyes out! Do you really imagine, Don Vanquished, Don Cudgeled, that I died for your sake? Everything you saw tonight was play-acting. I’m not the kind of woman to let so much as the black of my fingernail suffer for a camel like you, let alone die for one!”
“That I can easily believe,” said Sancho, “because all this business of lovers dying of heartbreak is nonsense. They may talk about it, but actually doing it — let Judas believe that!”

While they were talking, the musician, singer, and poet who had sung the two stanzas given above came in, and with a deep bow to Don Quixote he said, “Will your worship, sir knight, count and keep me among your most faithful servants? I have long been a great admirer of yours, as much for your fame as for your deeds.” “Will your worship tell me who you are,” Don Quixote replied, “so that my courtesy may match what you deserve?” The young man answered that he was the musician and singer of the night before. “Truly,” said Don Quixote, “your worship has an excellent voice; but what you sang did not strike me as very much to the point — for what have Garcilasso’s stanzas to do with this lady’s death?”

“Don’t let that surprise you,” the musician answered, “because among the green young poets of our day the custom is for everyone to write however he pleases and steal from wherever he chooses, whether it suits the subject or not; and nowadays there is no piece of foolishness they can sing or write that isn’t chalked up to poetic license.”

Don Quixote was about to reply, but the duke and duchess forestalled him by coming in to see him, and there followed a long and delightful conversation, in the course of which Sancho said so many droll and impudent things that he left the duke and duchess marveling at his simplicity and his sharpness in equal measure. Don Quixote asked their permission to leave that very day, since for a defeated knight like himself it was more fitting to live in a pigsty than in a royal palace. They granted it very willingly, and the duchess asked him whether Altisidora stood in his good graces.

He replied, “Señora, let me tell your ladyship that this young woman’s trouble comes entirely from idleness, and the cure for it is honest, steady occupation. She herself has told me that lace is worn in hell; and since she must know how to make it, let it never leave her hands. While she is busy moving the bobbins back and forth, the image — or images — of what she loves will not move back and forth in her thoughts. This is the truth, this is my opinion, and this is my advice.”

“And mine too,” added Sancho, “because in my whole life I’ve never seen a lace-maker die of love. When girls are at their work, their minds are more on finishing the job than on thinking about their sweethearts. I speak from my own experience: when I’m digging, I never think about my old woman — I mean my Teresa Panza, whom I love better than my own eyelids.” “Well said, Sancho,” said the duchess, “and I will see to it that from now on my Altisidora keeps herself busy with needlework of some kind, for she is extremely skilled at it.” “There is no need to resort to that remedy, señora,” said Altisidora, “because the mere thought of the cruelty this vagabond villain has shown me will be enough to wipe him from my memory without any other device. With your highness’s leave, I will withdraw, so as not to have before my eyes — I won’t say his rueful countenance — his hideous, ugly face.” “That reminds me of the old saying,” said the duke, “that ‘the one who rails is ready to forgive.’”
Altisidora then, pretending to dab away tears with a handkerchief, curtsied to her master and mistress and left the room.

“Bad luck go with you, poor girl,” said Sancho, “bad luck go with you! You’ve run into a soul as dry as a reed and a heart as hard as oak. If it had been me, by my faith, ‘a different rooster would have crowed for you.’”
With that the conversation ended, and Don Quixote dressed, dined with the duke and duchess, and set out that same evening.

title: Part 2, Chapter 71
paragraphs: What passed between Don Quixote and his squire Sancho on the way to their village

The defeated and dejected Don Quixote rode along very downcast on one count and very pleased on another. His gloom came from his defeat; his satisfaction came from thinking about the power that lay in Sancho, proved by the resurrection of Altisidora — though he had some trouble convincing himself that the lovesick young woman had actually been dead. Sancho, for his part, traveled in anything but good spirits, because it stung him that Altisidora had not kept her promise to give him the smocks; and turning this over in his mind, he said to his master, “Honestly, señor, I must be the unluckiest doctor in the world. Plenty of physicians kill the very patient they were supposed to cure and still expect to be paid for their work, though all they do is sign a little list of medicines that the apothecary, not they, makes up — and with that their labor is finished. But with me, curing somebody else costs me drops of blood, slaps, pinches, pinpricks, and whippings, and nobody gives me a penny. Well, I swear by all that’s good, if they put another patient into my hands, they’ll have to grease them first before I cure him; for, as they say, ‘it’s by his singing that the abbot earns his dinner,’ and I refuse to believe heaven gave me the gift I have just so I could hand it out to other people for nothing.”

“You are right, Sancho my friend,” said Don Quixote, “and Altisidora behaved very badly in not giving you the smocks she promised. And although that power of yours is _gratis data_ — since it has cost you no study at all, unless we count your bodily sufferings as study — I can say for my own part that if you had wanted payment for the lashes owed toward Dulcinea’s disenchantment, I would have paid you freely long before now. I am not certain, however, whether payment is compatible with the cure, and I would not want the reward to interfere with the medicine. Still, I think nothing is lost by trying it. Consider how much you want, Sancho, then whip yourself at once and pay yourself down in cash with your own hand, since you are carrying money of mine.”

At this proposal Sancho opened his eyes and ears a full hand’s breadth wide, and in his heart he very readily agreed to whip himself; and he said to his master, “Very well then, señor, I’ll hold myself ready to gratify your worship’s wishes, as long as I profit by it; love for my wife and children forces me to look like a greedy man. Tell me, your worship, how much you will pay me for every lash I give myself.”

“Sancho,” replied Don Quixote, “if I were to reward you as the importance and nature of this cure deserves, the treasures of Venice and the mines of Potosi would not be enough to pay you. See how much of mine you are carrying, and set a price on each lash.”

“The lashes,” said Sancho, “come to three thousand three hundred and some odd; of these I have given myself five, and the rest remain. Let the five cover the odd ones, and let us reckon the three thousand three hundred, which at a quarter real apiece — and I won’t take less though the whole world should bid against me — make three thousand three hundred quarter reals. The three thousand come to one thousand five hundred half reals, which make seven hundred and fifty reals; and the three hundred come to a hundred and fifty half reals, which amount to seventy-five reals, and those added to the seven hundred and fifty make eight hundred and twenty-five reals in all. These I will deduct from the money of your worship’s that I’m holding, and I’ll come home rich and content, though thoroughly whipped — for ‘there’s no catching trout’ — and I’ll say no more.”

“O blessed Sancho! O dear Sancho!” said Don Quixote. “How bound we shall be to serve you, Dulcinea and I, for all the days that heaven grants us! If she returns to her lost form — and it cannot be otherwise than that she will — her misfortune will have turned into good fortune, and my defeat into the happiest of triumphs. But tell me, Sancho: when will you begin the scourging? For if you make quick work of it, I’ll throw in a hundred reals over and above.”
“When?” said Sancho. “Tonight, without fail. Let your worship arrange for us to spend it outdoors in the open air, and I’ll flay myself raw.”

Night, which Don Quixote awaited with the greatest anxiety in the world, came at last, though it seemed to him that the wheels of Apollo’s chariot had broken down and that the day was stretching itself out longer than usual — just as happens with lovers, whose desires never agree with the clock’s reckoning. At length they made their way in among some pleasant trees standing a little way off the road, and there, emptying Rocinante’s saddle and Dapple’s pack-saddle, they stretched out on the green grass and supped from Sancho’s provisions. Sancho, fashioning a powerful, flexible whip out of Dapple’s halter and headstall, withdrew about twenty paces from his master in among some beech trees. Don Quixote, watching him march off with such resolution and spirit, said to him, “Take care, my friend, not to cut yourself to pieces; let the lashes wait their turn for one another, and don’t rush so fast that you run out of breath halfway — I mean, don’t lay on so hard that your life gives out before you reach the required number. And so that you don’t lose the game by a card too many or too few, I will stand apart and count the lashes you give yourself on this rosary of mine. May heaven help you as your good intention deserves.”

“‘A good payer isn’t troubled about leaving a pledge,’” said Sancho. “I intend to lay on in such a way that it hurts me without killing me — for in that, no doubt, lies the whole essence of this miracle.”

He then stripped himself to the waist, snatched up the rope, and began to lay on while Don Quixote counted the lashes. He had given himself perhaps six or eight when he began to think the joke no small matter and its price far too low; and pausing with his hand in the air, he told his master he was crying off on the grounds of a blind bargain, for every one of those lashes deserved to be paid at half a real, not a quarter.
“Carry on, Sancho my friend, and don’t lose heart,” said Don Quixote, “for I hereby double the stakes on the price.”

“In that case,” said Sancho, “God’s hand be in it, and let it rain lashes.” But the rogue stopped laying them on his own shoulders and laid into the trees instead, letting out groans every now and then so pitiful that you would have thought each one was tearing his soul up by the roots. Don Quixote, touched to the heart, and afraid Sancho might finish himself off and that through his squire’s recklessness he might lose his own object, said to him, “On your life, my friend, let the matter rest where it stands, for this remedy strikes me as a very harsh one, and it will be wise to have patience: ‘Zamora was not taken in an hour.’ If I have not miscounted, you have given yourself more than a thousand lashes; that is enough for now — for, to put it in homely terms, ‘the ass will carry the load, but not the overload.’”

“No, no, señor,” replied Sancho. “It will never be said of me, ‘The money pocketed, the arms broken.’ Step back a little farther, your worship, and let me give myself at least a thousand lashes more; in a couple of sessions like this we’ll have polished off the whole lot, and there will even be cloth left over.”
“Since you are in such a willing mood,” said Don Quixote, “may heaven assist you; lay on, and I will withdraw.”

Sancho went back to his task with such determination that he soon had the bark stripped off several trees — such was the severity with which he whipped himself; and once, raising his voice as he dealt a beech a tremendous stroke, he cried out, “Here dies Samson, and everyone with him!”

At the sound of his pitiful cry and the crack of the cruel lash, Don Quixote ran to him at once, seized the twisted halter that was serving as his scourge, and said, “Heaven forbid, Sancho my friend, that to please me you should lose your life, which is needed to support your wife and children. Let Dulcinea wait for a better opportunity; I will content myself with a hope soon to be fulfilled, and have patience until you have regained your strength, so that this business can be finished to everyone’s satisfaction.”

“Since your worship will have it so, señor,” said Sancho, “so be it; but throw your cloak over my shoulders, for I’m sweating and I don’t want to catch a chill — that’s a risk that novice flagellants run.”

Don Quixote did so, and stripping off his own cloak he covered Sancho, who slept until the sun woke him; then they continued their journey, which for the time being they broke off at a village three leagues farther on. They dismounted at a hostelry which Don Quixote recognized as exactly that, and did not take for a castle with moat, turrets, portcullis, and drawbridge; for ever since his defeat he had been talking more sensibly about everything, as will appear shortly. They lodged him in a ground-floor room, where instead of leather hangings there were pieces of painted serge of the kind commonly used in villages. On one of them, painted by some very clumsy hand, was the Rape of Helen, when the brazen guest carried her off from Menelaus; on the other was the story of Dido and Æneas, she on a high tower, as if signaling with half a bedsheet to her fugitive guest, who was out at sea fleeing in a frigate or a brigantine. He noticed that in the two stories Helen did not go with much reluctance, since she was laughing slyly and mischievously; but the fair Dido was shown shedding tears the size of walnuts. Looking at them, Don Quixote remarked, “Those two ladies were most unfortunate not to have been born in this age, and I most unfortunate of all men not to have been born in theirs. Had I encountered those gentlemen, Troy would never have been burned nor Carthage destroyed; I would only have had to kill Paris, and all these misfortunes would have been avoided.”

“I’ll bet,” said Sancho, “that before long there won’t be a tavern, roadside inn, hostelry, or barber’s shop where the story of our deeds isn’t painted up; but I’d want it painted by the hand of a better painter than the one who painted these.”

“You are right, Sancho,” said Don Quixote, “for this painter is like Orbaneja, a painter who lived in Úbeda; when people asked him what he was painting, he would answer, ‘Whatever it turns out to be,’ and if he happened to paint a cock he would write under it, ‘This is a cock,’ in case anyone thought it was a fox. The painter — or writer, for it comes to the same thing — who published the history of this new Don Quixote that has appeared must, I think, have been one of that sort, Sancho, for he painted or wrote ‘whatever it might turn out to be.’ Or perhaps he is like a poet named Mauleon who hung about the Court some years ago, who would answer at random whatever he was asked; when someone asked him what _Deum de Deo_ meant, he replied _Dé donde diere_. But setting all that aside, tell me, Sancho: do you feel like giving yourself another round tonight, and would you rather have it indoors or in the open air?”

“By heaven, señor,” said Sancho, “for what I’m planning to give myself, it’s all one to me whether it’s in a house or in the fields; still, I’d rather it were among trees, for I feel they keep me company and help me wonderfully to bear my pain.”

“And yet it must not be, Sancho my friend,” said Don Quixote; “rather, so that you can recover your strength, we must save it for our own village, for at the latest we shall arrive there the day after tomorrow.”

Sancho answered that his master might do as he pleased; but for his own part he would rather finish the business off quickly, while his blood was hot and he still had an appetite for it, because “there’s often danger in delay,” and “pray to God and keep swinging the hammer,” and “one ‘take this’ is worth more than two ‘I’ll give you’s,’” and “a sparrow in the hand is better than a vulture on the wing.”

“For God’s sake, Sancho, no more proverbs!” exclaimed Don Quixote. “It seems to me you are becoming _sicut erat_ again. Speak plainly, simply, and straightforwardly, as I have told you so often, and you will see how much good it does you.”

“I don’t know what bad luck of mine it is,” said Sancho, “but I can’t say a word without a proverb, and to my mind every proverb is as good as an argument; still, I’ll try to mend my ways if I can.” And with that, for the moment, the conversation ended.

title: Part 2, Chapter 72
paragraphs: How Don Quixote and Sancho came home to their village

Don Quixote and Sancho spent the whole of that day in the village and at the inn, waiting for nightfall — one of them so he could finish his whipping assignment out in the open country, the other so he could watch it completed, since the completion of it meant the fulfillment of all his hopes. While they waited, a traveler on horseback arrived at the inn with three or four servants, and one of these said to the man who seemed to be the master, “Señor Don Álvaro Tarfe, your worship can take your siesta here today; the rooms look clean and cool.”

Hearing this, Don Quixote turned to Sancho and said, “Listen, Sancho — when I was leafing through that book of the Second Part of my history, I believe I happened to come across this very name, Don Álvaro Tarfe.”
“Quite possibly,” said Sancho. “Let’s wait for him to dismount, and then we can ask him about it.”

The gentleman got down from his horse, and the landlady gave him a ground-floor room across from Don Quixote’s, hung with painted serge of the same kind. The newcomer changed into a summer coat and came out to the gateway of the inn, which was broad and cool, and seeing Don Quixote pacing back and forth there, he asked him, “Which way is your worship traveling, good sir?”
“To a village not far from here, which happens to be my own,” Don Quixote answered. “And your worship — where are you headed?”
“I am on my way to Granada, señor,” said the gentleman, “to my home country.”
“And a fine country it is,” said Don Quixote. “But would your worship do me the favor of telling me your name? Something tells me it matters more to me to know it than I can easily explain.”
“My name is Don Álvaro Tarfe,” the traveler replied.

To which Don Quixote answered, “Then I have not the slightest doubt that your worship is the Don Álvaro Tarfe who appears in print in the Second Part of the history of Don Quixote of La Mancha — the one recently printed and published by a new author.”

“I am that very man,” the gentleman replied, “and that Don Quixote, the main character of the history in question, was a close friend of mine. I was the one who drew him away from home — or at any rate persuaded him to attend some jousts being held at Saragossa, where I was going myself. The truth is, I did him many good turns, and I saved him from having his back stroked by the executioner for his reckless behavior.”
“Tell me, Señor Don Álvaro,” said Don Quixote, “do I resemble that Don Quixote you speak of in any way?”
“No indeed,” the traveler replied, “not in the least.”
“And that Don Quixote —” said ours, “did he have with him a squire named Sancho Panza?”
“He did,” said Don Álvaro, “but although he had a reputation for being very funny, I never once heard him say anything that was actually amusing.”

“That I can easily believe,” Sancho put in at this point, “because cracking jokes isn’t something just anyone can do, and that Sancho your worship is talking about, good sir, must be some monumental rogue, blockhead, and thief rolled into one. I am the real Sancho Panza, and I have more witty sayings in me than if it rained them. Just put me to the test — ride along with me for a year or so, and you’ll find they drop from me at every step, so rich and so abundant that, even though most of the time I don’t know what I’m saying, I set everyone who hears me laughing. And the real Don Quixote of La Mancha — the famous one, the valiant, the wise, the lover, the righter of wrongs, the guardian of minors and orphans, the protector of widows, the killer of damsels, he whose one and only mistress is the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso — is this gentleman standing here before you, my master. Every other Don Quixote and every other Sancho Panza is a dream and a fraud.”

“By God, I believe it,” said Don Álvaro, “because, my friend, you have produced more wit in the few words you have just spoken than the other Sancho Panza did in everything I ever heard out of him — and that was plenty. He was more glutton than talker, and more dull than funny; and I am now convinced that the enchanters who persecute Don Quixote the Good have set out to persecute me with Don Quixote the Bad. But I hardly know what to say, for I would swear I left him locked up in the Casa del Nuncio at Toledo, and yet here another Don Quixote appears before me — a very different one from mine.”

“Whether I am good, I cannot say,” said Don Quixote, “but I can say with confidence that I am not ‘the Bad.’ And as proof, let me tell you, Señor Don Álvaro Tarfe, that in my whole life I have never set foot in Saragossa. On the contrary, when I was told that this imaginary Don Quixote had appeared at the jousts in that city, I refused to enter it at all, precisely to expose his lie before the eyes of the whole world; and so I went straight on to Barcelona — that treasure-house of courtesy, refuge of strangers, shelter of the poor, homeland of the brave, avenger of the wronged, gracious meeting-place of firm friendships, a city without equal in situation and in beauty. And though what happened to me there is hardly material for pleasure — far more for regret — I do not regret it, simply because I have seen that city. In short, Señor Don Álvaro Tarfe, I am Don Quixote of La Mancha, the one fame speaks of, and not that wretched impostor who has tried to steal my name and dress himself up in my ideas. I beg your worship, by everything you owe to your standing as a gentleman, to be kind enough to make a sworn declaration before the alcalde of this village that you never in your life laid eyes on me until this moment, that I am not the Don Quixote printed in the Second Part, and that this Sancho Panza, my squire, is not the one your worship knew.”

“That I will do with the greatest pleasure,” Don Álvaro replied, “though it astonishes me to find two Don Quixotes and two Sancho Panzas at the same time, as alike in their names as they are unlike in their behavior. So I say again, and I solemnly declare, that what I saw I cannot have seen, and that what happened to me cannot have happened.”

“No doubt your worship is under an enchantment, like my lady Dulcinea del Toboso,” said Sancho, “and would to heaven your disenchantment depended on my giving myself another three thousand and some lashes like the ones I’m giving myself for her — I’d lay them on without asking anything in return.”
“I don’t follow this business about the lashes,” said Don Álvaro. Sancho answered that it was a long story, but he would gladly tell it if they happened to be traveling the same road.

By now it was time for dinner, and Don Quixote and Don Álvaro ate together. The village alcalde happened to come into the inn along with a notary, and Don Quixote presented a formal petition to him, setting out that it was necessary for the protection of his rights that Don Álvaro Tarfe, the gentleman there present, should declare before him that he did not know Don Quixote of La Mancha, likewise present, and that this was not the man who appeared in print in a history called “Second Part of Don Quixote of La Mancha, by a certain Avellaneda of Tordesillas.” In the end the alcalde drew it up in proper legal form, and the declaration was made with every formality such cases require — which left Don Quixote and Sancho delighted, as though a declaration of that kind mattered greatly to them, and as though their words and actions did not make the difference between the two Don Quixotes and the two Sanchos perfectly plain. Don Álvaro and Don Quixote exchanged many courtesies and offers of service, and in the course of them the great Manchegan showed such good judgment that he cured Don Álvaro of his mistake entirely; while Don Álvaro, for his part, came away persuaded that he must have been enchanted, now that he had touched, as it were, two Don Quixotes so utterly opposed.

Evening fell, and they left the village together; after about half a league the road forked, one branch leading to Don Quixote’s village, the other being the way Don Álvaro had to take. In that brief stretch Don Quixote told him about his unhappy defeat, and about Dulcinea’s enchantment and its remedy, all of which plunged Don Álvaro into fresh astonishment; and after embracing Don Quixote and Sancho, he went his way, and Don Quixote went his. That night they spent among trees again, so that Sancho might have the chance to carry out his penance — which he did exactly as he had the night before, at far greater cost to the bark of the beech trees than to his own back, which he protected so carefully that the lashes would not have dislodged a fly if one had been sitting there. The deceived Don Quixote kept count without missing a single stroke, and he reckoned that, together with those of the previous night, they came to three thousand and twenty-nine. The sun, it seemed, had risen early to witness the sacrifice, and by its light they took up their journey again, talking over the trick that had been played on Don Álvaro and congratulating themselves on having had his declaration taken before a magistrate in such unimpeachable form. They traveled that day and that night without anything worth recording happening to them — except that during the night Sancho completed his task, which filled Don Quixote with joy beyond all measure. He kept watching for daylight, to see whether along the road he might come upon his lady Dulcinea, now disenchanted; and as the journey went on, there was not a woman he passed whom he did not approach to see if she was Dulcinea del Toboso, for he held it absolutely certain that Merlin’s promises could not lie. Full of these thoughts and longings, they climbed a rise from which they caught sight of their own village, and at the sight of it Sancho dropped to his knees and cried, “Open your eyes, beloved home, and see your son Sancho Panza coming back to you — if not very rich, then very well whipped! Open your arms and receive your son Don Quixote too, who, though he comes conquered by another man’s arm, comes a conqueror over himself; and that, as he himself has told me, is the greatest victory anyone could wish for. I’m bringing money home, because if I took a good whipping, at least I rode like a gentleman.”

“Enough of this foolishness,” said Don Quixote. “Let us go straight on and reach our own home, where we can give our imaginations free rein and lay out the plans for the pastoral life we mean to lead.”
With that they came down the slope and made their way toward their village.

title: Part 2, Chapter 73
paragraphs: The omens Don Quixote encountered as he entered his own village, together with other incidents that adorn and brighten this great history

At the edge of the village, Cide Hamete tells us, Don Quixote came upon two boys arguing on the village threshing-floor, and one of them said to the other, “Don't wear yourself out, Periquillo; you'll never lay eyes on it again as long as you live.”
Don Quixote caught the words and turned to Sancho. “Did you notice, my friend, what that boy just said? ‘You'll never lay eyes on it again as long as you live.’”
“Well,” said Sancho, “what difference does it make that the boy said it?”
“What!” said Don Quixote. “Can't you see that if you apply those words to the object of my longing, they mean I am never to see Dulcinea again?”

Sancho was about to reply when something distracted him: a hare came tearing across the plain with a pack of greyhounds and huntsmen after it. Terrified, the animal bolted for cover and tried to hide itself under Dapple. Sancho scooped it up alive and held it out to Don Quixote, who was muttering, “_Malum signum, malum signum!_ A hare runs, greyhounds give chase, and Dulcinea does not appear.”

“Your worship is a strange one,” said Sancho. “Suppose we grant that this hare is Dulcinea, and that the greyhounds chasing her are the wicked enchanters who turned her into a peasant girl. She runs, I catch her and place her in your worship's hands, and you hold her in your arms and pet her — where is the bad sign in that? What sort of evil omen can anyone find here?”

The two quarrelling boys wandered over to look at the hare, and Sancho asked one of them what the fight had been about. The answer came from the one who had said “You'll never see it again as long as you live”: he had taken a cage full of crickets from the other boy and had no intention of returning it for the rest of his days. Sancho fished four cuartos out of his pocket, paid the boy for the cage, and placed it in Don Quixote's hands, saying, “There, señor! There are your omens, smashed and done away with; and to my mind — fool though I am — they have no more bearing on our affairs than last year's clouds. If I remember rightly, I've heard the curate of our village say that it ill becomes Christians or people of sense to pay attention to such nonsense; and indeed your worship told me the very same thing a while back — that any Christian who took notice of omens was a fool. So there's no point wasting words on it; let's press on and get into the village.”

The huntsmen rode up and asked for their hare, and Don Quixote handed it over. They continued on, and on the green at the entrance of the town they ran into the curate and the bachelor Samson Carrasco, occupied with their breviaries. It should be said that Sancho had draped over Dapple, by way of a pack-cloth, on top of the bundle of armour, the buckram robe painted with flames that had been put on him at the duke's castle the night Altisidora came back from the dead. He had also fitted the mitre onto Dapple's head — the strangest costume and transformation any donkey in the world has ever undergone. Both the curate and the bachelor recognised them at once and came toward them with arms outstretched. Don Quixote dismounted and embraced them warmly; and the village boys, who are lynxes from whom nothing is hidden, spotted the donkey's mitre and came running to look, shouting to one another, “Come and see, boys! Sancho Panza's donkey is decked out finer than Mingo, and Don Quixote's nag is skinnier than ever!”

And so at last, with the boys leaping about them and the curate and the bachelor at their side, they made their entry into the town and headed for Don Quixote's house, where they found the housekeeper and his niece waiting at the door, the news of his arrival having already reached them. Word had also been carried to Teresa Panza, Sancho's wife, and she — hair flying loose, half dressed, dragging her daughter Sanchica along by the hand — ran out to meet her husband. But when she saw him arriving in nothing like the style she imagined a governor should travel in, she said to him, “What's this, husband, coming home like this? You look to me as if you'd tramped the whole way on sore feet — more like a shiftless vagabond than a governor.”

“Quiet, Teresa,” said Sancho. “Often enough ‘where you find the pegs there's no bacon hanging on them.’ Let's go inside the house, and there you'll hear things to astonish you. I'm bringing money, which is what counts, and I earned it by my own labour without doing wrong to a soul.”
“Just you bring the money, my good husband,” said Teresa, “and never mind whether it came this way or that; however you came by it, you won't have invented any new custom in the world.”

Sanchica hugged her father and asked whether he had brought her anything, for she had been watching for him the way one watches for the rains of May; and with her holding on to his belt on one side, and his wife taking his hand, while the girl led Dapple, they set off for their house — leaving Don Quixote in his own, in the care of his niece and housekeeper and in the company of the curate and the bachelor.

Don Quixote, paying no heed to time or occasion, immediately drew the bachelor and the curate aside in private. In a few words he told them of his defeat, and of the obligation he was now under not to leave his village for a year — a pledge he intended to honour to the letter, without straying from it by a hair's breadth, as befitted a knight-errant bound by scrupulous good faith and the laws of knight-errantry. He explained that he was thinking of becoming a shepherd for that year and amusing himself in the solitude of the fields, where he could give his loving thoughts free rein while practising the virtuous pastoral calling; and he begged them, if they were not too busy and no weightier business stood in the way, to agree to be his companions, for he would buy enough sheep to qualify them all as shepherds. The most important part of the whole scheme, he told them, was already settled: he had picked out names for them that fitted like a glove. The curate asked what they were. Don Quixote answered that he himself would be called the shepherd Quixotize, the bachelor the shepherd Carrascon, the curate the shepherd Curambro, and Sancho Panza the shepherd Pancino.

The two of them were dumbfounded by Don Quixote's latest madness; but rather than risk his slipping away from the village once more in pursuit of his chivalry, and trusting that over the course of the year he might be cured, they went along with his new scheme, applauded his crazy notion as a stroke of brilliance, and offered to join him in the life. “What's more,” said Samson Carrasco, “as everyone knows, I am a very celebrated poet, and I'll be turning out verses at every opportunity — pastoral, or courtly, or whatever comes into my head — to pass the time in those lonely places where we'll be wandering. But the most essential thing, gentlemen, is for each of us to choose the name of the shepherdess he intends to celebrate in his verses, and for us never to leave a tree, however hard the bark, without writing and carving her name into it, as is the habit and custom of lovesick shepherds.”

“Exactly right,” said Don Quixote, “although I myself am spared the trouble of inventing an imaginary shepherdess, since I have the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso — the glory of these brookbanks, the ornament of these meadows, the pillar of beauty, the cream of every grace, and, in short, a being to whom all praise is fitting, however extravagant it may be.”
“Quite true,” said the curate; “but the rest of us will have to hunt up obliging shepherdesses who will suit our purposes one way or another.”

“And if they fail us,” added Samson Carrasco, “we can borrow the names of the printed ones the world is stuffed with — Fílidas, Amarilises, Dianas, Fleridas, Galateas, Belisardas. Since they're sold in the marketplaces, we may fairly buy them and make them our own. If my lady — or rather my shepherdess — should happen to be named Ana, I'll sing her praises under the name Anarda; if Francisca, I'll call her Francenia; if Lucia, Lucinda; it all amounts to the same thing. And Sancho Panza, if he joins this brotherhood, can celebrate his wife Teresa Panza under the name Teresaina.”

Don Quixote laughed at the fitting of the name, and the curate heaped praise on his worthy and honourable resolution, offering once again to keep him company whenever he could spare time from his pressing duties. With that they said their goodbyes, urging and begging him to look after his health and to eat what was good for him.

As it happened, his niece and the housekeeper had overheard everything the three of them said, and the moment the visitors were gone the two women came in to Don Quixote. “What's all this, uncle?” said the niece. “Just when we were thinking you'd come home to stay and live a quiet, respectable life here, do you mean to tangle yourself up in new schemes and go playing ‘young shepherd coming hither, young shepherd going hence’? No indeed — ‘the straw is too hard now for making pipes.’”

“And how,” the housekeeper added, “is your worship going to stand the summer heat out in the fields, and the winter cold, and the howling of the wolves? You won't; that's a life and a trade for tough men, raised and hardened to such work almost from the cradle. If you have to choose between evils, better a knight-errant than a shepherd! Look, señor, take my advice — and I give it not on a full stomach of bread and wine but fasting, and with fifty years on my head — stay at home, see to your affairs, go often to confession, be generous to the poor, and let it be on my soul if any harm comes to you.”

“That's enough, my daughters,” said Don Quixote. “I know perfectly well where my duty lies. Help me to bed, for I'm not feeling well; and you may be certain that, knight-errant today or wandering shepherd tomorrow, I shall never stop looking after your interests, as you'll see in the end.” And the good women (for good they undoubtedly were), the housekeeper and the niece, helped him to bed, where they brought him something to eat and made him as comfortable as they could.

title: Part 2, Chapter 74
paragraphs: How Don Quixote fell sick, the will he made, and how he died

Since nothing human lasts forever, and everything moves steadily downward from its beginning toward its end—human life above all—and since Don Quixote held no special dispensation from heaven to halt the course of his, his end and conclusion arrived when he least expected it. Whether it was the despondency brought on by brooding over his defeat, or simply heaven's will ordering it so, a fever took hold of him and kept him in bed for six days, during which his friends the curate, the bachelor, and the barber visited him often, while his good squire Sancho Panza never left his bedside. Convinced that what kept him in this state was grief at finding himself beaten, and at the failure of his heart's desire—the liberation and disenchantment of Dulcinea—they tried by every means in their power to lift his spirits. The bachelor urged him to take heart and get out of bed to begin his pastoral life, for which, he said, he had already composed an eclogue that would outshine everything Sannazaro had ever written, and had bought with his own money two famous dogs to guard the flock, one called Barcino and the other Butron, sold to him by a herdsman of Quintanar.

Even so, Don Quixote could not shake off his sadness. His friends sent for the doctor, who took his pulse, was not much pleased with what he found, and said that, whatever else happened, he would do well to attend to the health of his soul, since that of his body was in danger. Don Quixote received this calmly; not so his housekeeper, his niece, and his squire, who began weeping bitterly, as though he already lay dead before them. The doctor's judgment was that melancholy and despondency were bringing his life to its close. Don Quixote asked them to leave him alone, as he wished to sleep a little. They obeyed, and he slept, as the saying goes, at one stretch for more than six hours—so long that the housekeeper and the niece thought he would never wake again. But at the end of that time he did wake, and cried out in a loud voice, “Blessed be Almighty God, who has shown me such goodness! Truly his mercies have no limit, and the sins of men can neither narrow them nor hold them back!”

The niece listened closely to her uncle's words, and they struck her as more coherent than anything he usually said, at least since his illness began, so she asked, “What are you saying, señor? Has something new happened? What mercies are these, and what sins of men are you talking about?”

“The mercies, niece,” said Don Quixote, “are those God has shown me at this very moment—mercies, as I said, that my sins have done nothing to obstruct. My mind is now free and clear, released from the dark shadows of ignorance that my wretched, ceaseless reading of those detestable books of chivalry had cast over it. Now I see their absurdities and deceptions for what they are, and my only sorrow is that this awakening has come so late that it leaves me no time to make some amends by reading other books that might be a light to my soul. Niece, I feel that I am at the point of death, and I want to meet it in a way that shows my life was not so bad that I must leave behind me the reputation of a madman; for though I have been one, I would rather the fact not be made plainer by my dying. Call my good friends in to me, my dear: the curate, the bachelor Samson Carrasco, and Master Nicholas the barber, for I wish to confess and make my will.” His niece was spared the errand, for at that moment all three of them walked in. The instant Don Quixote saw them he exclaimed, “Good news for you, good sirs: I am no longer Don Quixote of La Mancha, but Alonso Quixano, whose way of life earned him the name of Good. I am now the enemy of Amadis of Gaul and of the whole countless tribe of his descendants; every profane story of knight-errantry is hateful to me now; now I recognize my folly, and the danger that reading them led me into; and now, brought back to my right mind by God's mercy, I detest them.”

When the three of them heard him speak this way, they felt certain some new madness had taken hold of him; and Samson said, “What is this, Señor Don Quixote? Now, just when we have news that the lady Dulcinea is disenchanted, you take this line? Now, when we are on the very point of becoming shepherds, to spend our lives singing like princes, you want to turn hermit? Be quiet, for heaven's sake; come back to yourself and let's have no more of this nonsense.”

“All that nonsense,” said Don Quixote, “which until now has been real enough to do me harm, my death, with heaven's help, will turn to my good. I feel, sirs, that death is coming on quickly. Enough joking; bring me a confessor to hear my confession and a notary to draw up my will, for at a moment like this a man cannot trifle with his soul. So while the curate hears my confession, let someone go for the notary, I beg you.”

They looked at one another, astonished at Don Quixote's words; yet, uncertain as they were, they inclined to believe him. And one of the signs that led them to conclude he was dying was precisely this sudden and complete return to his senses after so long a madness; for to the words already quoted he added many more, so well expressed, so devout, and so reasonable, that their doubts vanished and they were convinced his mind was sound. The curate sent everyone out, stayed alone with him, and heard his confession. The bachelor went for the notary and came back shortly afterward with him and with Sancho Panza, who—having already learned from the bachelor what condition his master was in, and finding the housekeeper and the niece in tears—began to sob and weep himself.
When the confession was over, the curate came out and said, “Alonso Quixano the Good is truly dying, and he is truly in his right mind. We may go in to him now while he makes his will.”

This news gave a tremendous push to the already brimming eyes of the housekeeper, the niece, and Sancho Panza, his good squire, so that tears burst from their eyes and a whole chorus of sighs from their hearts; for in truth, as has been said more than once, whether as plain Alonso Quixano the Good or as Don Quixote of La Mancha, he was always gentle in temper and kind in all his dealings, and for that reason he was loved not only by his own household but by everyone who knew him.

The notary came in with the others, and once the preamble of the will had been drawn up and Don Quixote had commended his soul to God with all the customary devotions, he came to the bequests and said, “Item: it is my will that, concerning certain monies in the hands of Sancho Panza—whom in my madness I made my squire—since various accounts, debits, and credits have passed between him and me, no claim shall be brought against him, nor any reckoning demanded of him on that score; and if anything remains after he has paid himself what I owe him, the balance, which will not be much, shall be his, and may it do him much good. And if, when I was mad, I had a part in giving him the governorship of an island, now that I am in my senses I would give him the governorship of a kingdom if I could, for the simplicity of his nature and the faithfulness of his conduct deserve it.” Then, turning to Sancho, he said, “Forgive me, my friend, for making you seem as mad as I was, and for drawing you into the same error I fell into myself—the belief that there were, and still are, knights-errant in the world.”

“Ah, don't die, master!” said Sancho through his tears. “Take my advice and live a great many years; for the most foolish thing a man can do in this life is to let himself die for no rhyme or reason, with nobody killing him and no hands finishing him off but melancholy's. Come on, don't be lazy: get up from that bed and let's head for the fields dressed as shepherds, the way we agreed. Who knows—behind some bush we may find the lady Dulcinea disenchanted, as fine a sight as anyone could wish. If it's grief at being beaten that's killing you, put the blame on me and say you were knocked down because I girthed Rocinante badly; besides, your worship must have seen in your books of chivalry that it's the commonest thing in the world for knights to unseat one another, and for the man beaten today to be the winner tomorrow.”
“Quite true,” said Samson, “and good Sancho Panza has exactly the right view of these matters.”

“Not so fast, sirs,” said Don Quixote. “‘In last year's nests there are no birds this year.’ I was mad, and now I am in my senses; I was Don Quixote of La Mancha, and now, as I said, I am Alonso Quixano the Good. May my repentance and my sincerity restore me to the esteem you once had for me—and now let Master Notary continue.

“Item: I leave my entire estate, without restriction, to Antonia Quixana, my niece, here present, after deducting from the most readily available portion of it whatever is needed to satisfy the bequests I have made. And the first payment I want made is the wages I owe my housekeeper for the time she has served me, with twenty ducats over and above for a gown. As my executors I appoint the curate and the bachelor Samson Carrasco, here present.

“Item: it is my wish that if my niece, Antonia Quixana, should want to marry, she marry a man about whom inquiry has first been made to establish that he does not know what books of chivalry are; and if it turns out that he does know, and my niece insists on marrying him anyway, and does marry him, then she shall forfeit everything I have left her, and my executors shall devote it to works of charity as they see fit.

“Item: I beg those same gentlemen, my executors, that if some happy chance should lead them to discover the author said to have written a history now circulating under the title ‘Second Part of the Achievements of Don Quixote of La Mancha,’ they ask him on my behalf, as earnestly as they can, to forgive me for having been, without ever intending it, the cause of his writing so many and such enormous absurdities as that book contains; for I leave this world with a troubled conscience at having given him the occasion to write them.”

With that he closed the will, and, a faintness coming over him, he stretched out at full length on the bed. Everyone was alarmed and hurried to his aid, and during the three days he lived after making his will he fainted again and again. The whole house was in an uproar; and yet the niece went on eating, the housekeeper drank, and Sancho Panza kept his spirits up—for inheriting something erases, or at least softens, in the heir the grief the dead man might reasonably be expected to leave behind.

At last Don Quixote's end came, after he had received all the sacraments and had denounced books of chivalry in full and forceful terms. The notary happened to be present, and he remarked that in no book of chivalry had he ever read of a knight-errant dying in his bed so calmly and in so Christian a manner as Don Quixote, who, amid the tears and laments of everyone there, gave up his spirit—that is to say, died. Seeing this, the curate asked the notary to bear witness that Alonso Quixano the Good, commonly called Don Quixote of La Mancha, had passed from this present life and died a natural death; he wanted this testimony, he said, to remove any possibility that some author other than Cide Hamete Benengeli might falsely bring him back to life and spin endless stories out of his deeds.

Such was the end of the Ingenious Gentleman of La Mancha, whose village Cide Hamete declined to name precisely, so that all the towns and villages of La Mancha might compete among themselves for the right to adopt him and claim him as their son, just as the seven cities of Greece contended over Homer. The weeping of Sancho, the niece, and the housekeeper is left out here, along with the new epitaphs set upon his tomb; Samson Carrasco, however, wrote these lines:
Here lies a gentleman of mettle, a stranger all his life to fear; not even in his final hour, with Death upon him, could Death contrive to make him cower.
For the world he cared but little, and the world stood frightened at his feats; he passed his life as one gone mad, but died at last with his mind made whole.

And the most sage Cide Hamete said to his pen, “Rest here, hung from this rack by this brass wire, O my pen—whether finely cut or clumsily trimmed, I cannot say—and here you shall stay for long ages to come, unless presumptuous or malicious storytellers take you down to profane you. But before they lay a hand on you, warn them, and tell them, as well as you are able:
Hands off, you weaklings—hold your hands! Let no one dare attempt it; for this exploit, my lord the king, was reserved for me alone.

For me alone was Don Quixote born, and I for him; his part was to act, mine to write; the two of us together are but one, whatever that pretended Tordesillan writer may claim—the one who dared, or may yet dare, to record the deeds of my valiant knight with his great, coarse, badly trimmed ostrich quill. The task is no burden for his shoulders, no subject for his frozen wit; and should you ever happen to meet him, warn him to leave the weary, mouldering bones of Don Quixote at rest where they lie, and not to try, against all the privileges of death, to carry him off to Old Castile, raising him from the grave where he really and truly lies stretched at full length, powerless to make any third expedition or fresh sally. For the two he has already made—so much to the delight and approval of everyone who came to know of them, in this country and abroad—are quite enough to turn into ridicule the whole parade of sallies made by the whole tribe of knights-errant. In doing this you will discharge your Christian calling, giving good counsel to one who wishes you ill. And I shall remain satisfied and proud to have been the first author ever to enjoy the fruit of his writings as fully as he could desire; for my one desire has been to deliver over to mankind's contempt the false and foolish tales of the books of chivalry, which, thanks to the story of my true Don Quixote, are already tottering and will doubtless fall, never to rise again. Farewell.”
